title: Poems and stories
intro: 36 reading questions are built on a poem and 111 on a novel, a short story or a play. Most ask for a purpose or a structure, what a word means, or a quotation that fits a claim. They are not the hard ones: College Board rates 14% of the poem questions and 24% of the story questions Hard, against 38% of the other reading questions, and question type by question type they are rated Hard about as often as the rest or less often.
poem: Read by sentence, not by line. The test prints a poem with its line breaks, but the thought runs on past them: where the bank marks the breaks, 141 of 154 lines end in the middle of a sentence. Pause where the punctuation tells you to, and put each sentence in plain words before you read the next.

Find the turn. A short poem often does one thing and then another: a scene, then what the speaker makes of it; a charge, then an answer. A but, a then, a dash or a sudden question often marks the spot. 3 of the 5 questions on a poem’s overall structure have a right answer of the form “this, then that,” and in each of them all four choices take that form, so find the turn first and check both halves. In “Black Finger” the speaker describes a cypress against a gold sky, then asks what it means.

Name the speaker’s attitude. Ask how the speaker feels about what the poem shows, and whether the feeling changes at the turn. All 8 main idea and main purpose questions on a poem have a right answer about a feeling or a view: longing, regret, praise, encouragement.

When an image stands for an idea, say the idea plainly and stay close to the words. The right answer translates the picture and adds nothing. In “Hymn III” the mind is like a flower because both thrive when they are fed and wilt when they are not, and the answer says just that: it needs proper nourishment to thrive. One wrong choice takes the poem’s dew and rain literally and says the mind draws strength from the weather. In “Thoughts in a Zoo” people are caged like the lion, and the answer is that they have hopes their limits keep them from reaching.
story: Read for what a character feels, wants or is like. That is the Feeling tag, and most story questions turn on it: in 19 of the 27 main idea and main purpose questions on a story, the right answer is about what a character feels, wants, thinks or is like (Heidi is delighted by a picture, Francie is set on a goal, Mary is happy in the garden). Most of the rest describe a scene or what someone does or says.

Translate the old wording as you go. 61 of the 90 story passages and 20 of the 22 poem passages come from works published before 1925. Swap in plain words as you read; Names, brackets and old words shows how.
